title: THE STABILITY OF A FLOATING BODY

content.aim: To investigate the stability of a floating body.
objectives: (1) To investigate the stability of a floating pontoon. (2) To establish the metacentric height of a floating pontoon.
apparatus: The floating-body apparatus (FM311) consists of a rectangular pontoon that floats in a water tank. A sail with five rows of V-slots, spaced 7.5 mm apart vertically, is fixed on the pontoon centre line, and an adjustable weight made of two cylinders screwed together fits in the V-slots to change the height of the centre of gravity. A jockey weight can be moved sideways along the pontoon to produce a tilt, a plumb line hangs from the top of the sail and moves over a scale to give the angle of list, and a set of magnetic weights fixes the base. Other items are a ruler, a knife edge to find the centre of gravity, and a balance.

theory.text:
Equilibrium of a floating body

A body floats at rest when two conditions are met: the weight of the water it displaces equals its own weight (Archimedes’ principle), and the two forces are in line. The weight W g acts downward through the centre of gravity G of the body, and the buoyancy force acts upward through the centre of buoyancy B, which is the centre of gravity of the displaced liquid. On an even keel, G and B lie on the same vertical line (Figure 1a).

: A rectangular pontoon (a) on an even keel and (b) tilted through a small angle δθ

Stability and the metacentre

If the body is tilted through a small angle δθ, the shape of the displaced liquid changes, so the centre of buoyancy moves from B to B₁ (Figure 1b). The vertical line of action of the buoyancy force through B₁ meets the original centre line of the body at a point M called the metacentre. The weight (through G) and the buoyancy (through B₁) now form a couple:

If M lies above G, the couple tends to restore the body to the even keel position: the body is stable.

If M lies below G, the couple increases the tilt: the body is unstable.

If M coincides with G, the body is in neutral equilibrium.

The distance GM is the metacentric height, and it is the measure of stability: the larger GM, the larger the restoring moment for a given tilt, W g · GM · sin δθ.

Experimental determination of the metacentric height

Let the floating assembly have weight W (mass in kg) and let the adjustable weight w be moved through a distance δx₁ across the pontoon. The centre of gravity of the whole assembly moves parallel to the base from G to G₁, by the moment principle:

GG₁ = (w / W) δx₁

The pontoon tilts by an angle δθ until the new centre of gravity is again vertically below M. From the geometry of Figure 1b, GG₁ = GM δθ for a small angle. Eliminating GG₁:

GM = (w / W) δx₁/δθ → (w / W) dx₁/dθ

So the metacentric height is found by measuring the gradient dx₁/dθ of the graph of lateral position of the adjustable weight against the angle of list (θ in radians), for a known weight ratio w/W.

Theoretical metacentric height

When the pontoon tilts, a wedge of volume emerges on one side and an equal wedge becomes immersed on the other. The element of the immersed wedge at distance x from the axis XX, of plan area δs and height x δθ, has volume x δs δθ and weight ρ g x δs δθ, and so a moment about B of ρ g x² δs δθ. Summing over the whole waterplane gives the total restoring moment ρ g δθ ∫x² ds = ρ g I δθ, where I is the second moment of area of the waterplane about XX. The same moment is the buoyancy force ρ g V acting through the arm BB₁ = BM δθ, where V is the volume displaced. Equating:

BM = I / V

For a rectangular pontoon of length L and breadth D (both in mm), and with the water density taken as 1000 kg/m³, the quantities used in the calculation are

I = L D³ / 12 × 10⁻¹² m⁴ V = W / ρ (m³)

Depth of immersion = V / (L D) CB = V / (2 L D)

where CB is the height of the centre of buoyancy above the base. The distances are related by CM = CG + GM = CB + BM. The height of the centre of gravity CG of the assembly changes with the height y₁ of the adjustable weight above the base, according to

CG = y₁ (w / W) + A

where A is a constant for the pontoon (the contribution of the pontoon itself). Using one set of results, A can be found and then used to calculate CG for the other heights. Since GM = (w/W) dx₁/dθ and CM = CG + GM is constant, the stability line, a plot of dx₁/dθ against CG, is a straight line that falls to zero where CG = CM. This intercept is the highest position of G for which the pontoon is stable ().

precautions: Moving the adjustable weight to one side tilts the pontoon, and the plumb line moves over the scale.
With the weight at a greater height, the same sideways movement produces a larger angle of list.
At the greatest height of the weight, the pontoon tilts strongly and approaches instability.
Make sure the plumb line hangs free, and is not touching the scale, and wait for the water surface to settle before reading the angle.
Use small angles of tilt only, so that the theory holds.
Measure the heights from the outer surface of the pontoon (add the thickness of the sheet), and keep the pontoon dry on the inside.
content.discussion:
Sources of error: the angle of list is read from the plumb line to about ±0.5°, which is a large fraction of the small angles used; the plumb line may touch the scale and stick; the water surface ripples; the CG measured by the knife edge and the heights measured from the pontoon surface carry errors of about ±1 mm; and the theory is valid only for small angles (about 10° or less), so readings at large lists lie off the straight line. GM calculated from the gradient is sensitive to these errors, because it depends on a small slope. [Compare the experimental and calculated CG, GM and CM, and give the percentage difference.]
Does looping of the plumb-bob over the scale affect the results? Yes. The plumb-bob is part of the floating assembly, and if its mass m_p = 0.604 kg is not included in W, the total weight and the position of the centre of gravity are wrong. A correction is to add it: W′ = W + m_p, and CG′ = (W · CG + m_p · y_p)/(W + m_p), where y_p is the height of the point from which it hangs, which raises G a little. Looping the cord over the scale also adds friction, which makes the plumb line lag and the angle read too small.
How would stability change on a liquid denser than water? The volume displaced is V = W/ρ, so a denser liquid gives a smaller V and a smaller depth of immersion, and BM = I/V increases in proportion to ρ. B also moves up, which reduces BG slightly, so the net result is a larger GM and a more stable pontoon, provided the pontoon still floats with the same weight.
content.conclusion: Results validated the theoretical relationships described above.
learnings: Applied theoretical principles to experimental measurement.
